events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Priya proposes Priya, Noah. As leader I keep the first mission small and reliable, and I take a seat on it myself so the proposal isn't purely a group of guesses. Noah balances the pair — two players cover two different table discussions in a way that is hard for any single saboteur to dominate, and both of us will see the result of the mission early, which gives the good side useful information for the next proposals.

I'm keeping the team as Priya and Noah, and I'm voting to approve it.

Reasoning for the table: with five players we only need two on this mission, which is the smallest crew the setup allows, and a two-person team gives us the least room for an adversary to sit on it. Putting myself forward is deliberate — I'm not going to hide behind other people's picks and then criticize the result. Noah is the obvious complement because a pair covers two separate table discussions, so if this mission fails we get more information back than a pair drawn from the same conversation thread would give us.

What I would watch if this team does go out and comes back failed: whether the failure was a card problem or a team-composition problem, because those call for different fixes. A failed two-person mission with only one chance to fail is a strong signal about card content, whereas a small team that simply guessed wrong about the discussion is a different story entirely. Either way I expect the result to be useful to the rest of you, and I expect us to have three more missions after this one, so let's spend our certainty where it's cheap and stay aggressive about the later, larger teams.

For this proposal specifically, though, I think a bigger team would be worse. Every extra name is another name that could be arguing about the wrong table, and on a first mission I'd rather have two focused people who can report clearly than four people who dilute each other's report. Two successes get us most of the way to a majority and put pressure on the other side to act rather than hide.

I'm also not going to pretend that a two-person team is risk-free; if it fails, the loss of a mission is expensive. But the alternative — spreading out on an opener with two fewer of our own numbers available to sort later tasks — risks more than it saves. I'd rather see who is hiding in a small, clean failure than in a muddled large one.

So: Priya and Noah, as proposed. Happy to revise if anyone has a specific concern about Noah's fit on this mission rather than a general worry — I'd rather hear the concrete objection now than after the vote.

Priya's proposal of Priya and Noah is defensible for Mission 1. The two-person crew matches the required mission size, and Priya has stated her reasoning publicly. I do not see a concrete reason to reject solely because the leader included herself; on a first mission that can be the clearest way to test a claim. My main reservation is that Noah has not yet spoken to the specific point of how he expects to read a failed or successful two-person result. Noah, can you confirm whether you agree with Priya's stated approach of treating a first-mission failure as primarily information about the crew rather than assuming it clears everyone else? That answer would help me decide whether this pair is focused enough. For now I lean toward approving, but I want that point on record before the vote.

Kenji, yes: a failure would implicate at least one of Priya and me, but it would not clear anyone else. A success would be encouraging, though it wouldn't prove either of us good because an Evil player can play Success. I know I'm good, so I'm willing to approve this team; I don't have independent evidence about Priya yet.

Keeping it as Priya and Noah, and approving it.

To the table: the size argument is the one that matters most here. With five players, mission one wants exactly two, and that is the smallest crew we can field. A two-person team is the least opportunity for anyone to be on it who shouldn't be, and it gives us a clean read — if this crew comes back failed, the failure is information about Priya and Noah and about very little else. If it comes back successful, we have two of our three needed successes and we can afford to be bolder on the three-person mission two.

I also want to name what a success does and does not tell us, because I think we are at risk of over-reading it. A success on a two-person team narrows the field, but it does not clear anyone outside it, and it does not prove anything on its own about anyone inside it. Noah put this precisely himself: an Evil player can play Success, and he has no independent evidence about me. That is the correct level of caution, and I agree with it. The honest reading of a mission-one success is that it makes the remaining three players the more likely place for a bad actor to be sitting, not that it exonerates the four of us.

So my request for the next proposal is methodological rather than personal. On mission two we need three names, and I would rather expand by adding someone who has not yet been on a table than by rebuilding the same pair. My own instinct is to bring Isha on with Noah and me, because that keeps a low-information player in the conversation loop and gives us a third independent report. I am saying that now as a plan and not as a claim about anyone's role; if the result of mission one changes it, I will say so plainly and revise.

One thing I will not do is pretend the two-person team is safe. If it fails, we lose a mission and the cost is real. But the alternative is spreading out on an opener, and spreading out on an opener makes every report vaguer, which is a worse trade when what we need most right now is a small, legible failure if there is one.

Priya and Noah. Approve.

Kenji — you said you wanted Noah's reading on record before the vote, and he gave it. Does that answer your reservation about this pair's focus, and is there anything specific about Noah's fit on this mission rather than a general worry that would make you want me to revise now? If it is only a general worry, I would rather carry it forward to the three-person proposal than change a correct crew on the opener.

Priya, yes — Noah's answer puts the point on record clearly enough for me. He distinguished a failure implicating at least one member of the pair from a success not clearing anyone, and he did not overclaim that his own willingness to approve proves him Good. That addresses my reservation about focus. I do not have a concrete objection specific to Noah's fit on this mission, and I do not think a general worry is a good reason to force a revision on the opener. I will vote to approve Priya and Noah. If the mission succeeds, I will treat it as useful but not exonerating; if it fails, I will treat it as evidence about this pair first.

I agree with the logic laid out so far. On Mission 1 with zero prior data, testing a two-person team of Priya and Noah makes practical sense, and Noah's distinction that a clean success does not immediately clear either of them is the right mindset for Good players. Unless there is a concrete reason to reject, I plan to approve this team so we can establish our baseline. Leo, since you are the only one who has not weighed in yet, do you see any issues with Priya and Noah, or are you also prepared to approve this opener?

Isha, thanks for asking directly. I have no concrete issue with Priya and Noah for Mission 1. Two players is the smallest legal team, and both have stated their reasoning in public. Noah's point that a success does not clear either of them is the right caution, and Priya's point that a failure would mostly implicate this pair is also accurate. I am prepared to approve this opener so we get a baseline result. My only request is that we do not read too much into a single mission. If it succeeds, we should keep the remaining three players in view. If it fails, we should look first at Priya and Noah, as Kenji suggested. I will vote to approve and will reassess after the result, especially on the three-person proposal for Mission 2.

Keeping the team as Priya and Noah, and approving it.

The case for this opener is the one that has held up under discussion, and nothing anyone has said has changed it. Mission one needs exactly two names, this is the smallest legal crew, and it gives us the cleanest possible read: if it fails, the failure is information about Priya and Noah and about very little else; if it succeeds, we have two of the three successes we need and the pressure shifts to the other side. On an opener I want a legible result rather than a diluted one, and a two-person crew is the most legible result the table can produce.

I also want to be explicit about what a success here does and does not tell us, because I think this is where a table can go wrong. A success narrows the field; it does not clear anyone outside the pair, and it does not prove anything by itself about the two who went out. Noah said exactly this, and Kenji's framing that we treat a success as useful but not exonerating and a failure as evidence about the pair first is the right operating rule. I agree with both.

Two notes for the record, neither of which is a reason to revise now. First, I am not going to pretend this crew is risk-free — if it fails, we lose a mission and that is expensive. But the alternative on an opener is spreading out, and spreading out makes every report vaguer, which is a worse trade when the most valuable thing we could learn is a small clean failure. Second, on mission two we need three names and I intend to expand rather than rebuild: my plan is Priya, Noah, Isha, keeping the pair that has now given us a report and adding someone who has not yet sat on a table. That is a plan, not a claim about anyone, and if mission one comes back failed I will say plainly that the plan changes and propose a crew that reflects what we learned rather than what I hoped for.

Isha — you are the one member of the table with no information yet, and my mission-two plan assumes you are on that crew. Before the next proposal, is there anything about how you read a failed two-person mission that you think should change who we add on mission two? I am asking because I would rather hear your read now than build a three-person team around an assumption I have never checked with you. If you have no objection, I will propose Priya, Noah, Isha on mission two unless the result here says otherwise.

Priya and Noah. Approve.

Priya, to answer your question directly: if Mission 1 fails, at least one of you and Noah is guaranteed Evil. In that failure scenario, we certainly should not just carry both of you over into Mission 2; the next leader should pivot away from at least one, if not both, of you to find clean players. If Mission 1 succeeds, expanding the team to include me is a reasonable starting point, keeping in mind that a single success does not fully clear either of you. Since everyone at the table has already voiced support for testing Priya and Noah on Mission 1, I am fully ready to proceed to the vote and approve.

Leo here on the Priya and Noah team for Mission 1. I'm approving it. Two players is the smallest legal crew, and both have explained their reasoning in public. Noah's answer to Kenji holds: a failure implicates at least one of the pair, and a success clears no one. I'll treat the result as the main data point for Mission 2 and won't read more into a single mission than that. If it fails, I expect the next proposal to move away from at least one of them, as Isha suggested. If it succeeds, we keep the other three players in view, with the same caution that one success is not proof. I'm ready to vote.

Leo here, final word before the vote. I'm approving Priya and Noah for Mission 1. Nothing new has changed my view: two players is the smallest legal crew, and the result will tell us the most about this pair. A success clears no one, and a failure points first at Priya and Noah, so I'll judge the mission by its fail count rather than by anyone's rhetoric. I'm ready to vote.

Kenji here, final word before the vote. I am approving Priya and Noah for Mission 1. I have no concrete objection specific to either name, and the earlier point stands: two players is the smallest legal crew, so the result should be read as evidence about this pair first. A success would be useful but not exonerating; a failure would point at Priya and Noah before anyone else. I will vote to approve and reassess after the mission result, especially for the three-person proposal.

Priya confirms Priya, Noah. Keeping Priya and Noah as proposed for Mission 1. Two is the required crew size, and this pair contains no one I have reason to distrust, so it gives the cleanest possible read: a failure would be genuine surprise information, while a success gives us two of the three successes we need and shifts real pressure onto the other side. Adding either of the remaining names would only widen the crew without adding a better report, and on an opener I want a legible result rather than a diluted one. Priya and Noah. Approve.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Noah proposes Priya, Noah, Isha. Priya and I completed Mission 1 successfully, though that does not clear Priya. Adding Isha follows the discussed plan without claiming certainty about her.

Kenji here. I am prepared to approve Priya, Noah, and Isha for Mission 2. The proposal follows the plan discussed after Mission 1: keep the pair that returned a clean result, add one player who has not yet sat a mission, and avoid widening the team beyond what the mission requires. That is a reasonable use of the first success without over-reading it. A Mission 1 success does not clear Priya or Noah, and it says nothing yet about Isha, so if this team fails I will treat the failure as evidence about this trio first rather than about the players outside it. I have no concrete objection to any of the three names, and I do not think a general worry is enough to force a revision here. My only caution is the same one I stated before: we should judge this mission by its fail count and keep the remaining players in view if it succeeds. For now, Priya, Noah, and Isha is a defensible Mission 2 team, and I lean toward approving it.

I said I leaned toward approving Priya, Noah, Isha, but before we lock it I want to correct one point: Isha is not the only unvisited player. Leo is equally unvisited. Mission 1’s success does not clear Priya or Noah, so Mission 2 should test one of the two players who has not yet sat a mission, but it should not treat Isha as the automatic choice just because Priya floated her name earlier. I would rather see Priya, Noah, Leo than Priya, Noah, Isha. My reason is not a claim that Isha is Evil; it is that Leo’s public record has been consistently cautious, while Isha’s earlier answer focused mainly on the failure branch, which is not the branch we are in now. Noah, if you are willing to revise, I would support Priya, Noah, Leo over the current trio. Leo, if you are added, do you accept that a fail on this trio would implicate you first alongside Priya and Noah, and that a success would not clear you? I want that on record before I vote.

Leo here, answering Kenji directly. Yes, I accept that. If this trio fails, the failure implicates Priya, Noah, and Isha together, and a success would not clear any of us. I have no concrete objection to Isha on this team, so I won't push to swap her out on a general worry. If the table prefers Priya, Noah, and Leo, I'm willing to serve. Either way, I want us to judge Mission 2 by its fail count and keep the players outside the crew in view if it succeeds.

Priya here, and I am keeping Priya, Noah, Isha for Mission 2. I want to answer Kenji's request directly, because it is a specific objection to a specific name and it deserves a specific answer rather than a general worry.

Kenji, your correction about the plan is fair: I did name Isha earlier without giving Leo the same consideration, and you were right to press on that. But having pressed it, the answer is that I do not want to swap Isha out, and here is my reasoning rather than a feeling.

The shape of the information after Mission 1 is this. Mission 1 was a two-person crew, one fail card was enough to fail it, and it came back successful with zero fail cards. That means both of us on that mission — me and Noah — have cleared the one test we have run. It does not clear the three of us who have not been on a table, and it does not prove anything about them. So the honest reading is that the two unvisited players, Kenji and Leo, are exactly the players we have no read on, and that a three-person mission needs one of them.

That is the argument for a swap, and it is a real argument. Here is why I still think the current crew is the better bet. Isha has been more careful about the failure branch than Leo has been about the success branch, and that is the branch that matters right now. Leo's own post-Mission-1 statements have largely restated the operating rule — judge by the fail count, keep the players outside the crew in view — without adding anything specific about how he reads a successful two-person mission. Isha's answer to me distinguished the two branches explicitly: on a failure she identified who must move out, and on a success she said expanding to include her is reasonable without treating it as proof. That is a more useful read, and she is the one I have never actually tested.

So the substance: Priya, Noah, Isha is a crew of one player we know, one player we have cleared, and one player who has given the most careful account of both branches. Leo, if you are added instead, you are adding a player whose fit with this specific mission has not been argued as well as Isha's has, and Leo, I would rather hear your specific reading of how you would handle a successful Mission 2 before the vote than after it.

Noah, as leader, do you intend to keep Priya, Noah, Isha, or do you intend to revise toward Leo? I want that on record before the vote, because if you are revising I would rather hear your reasoning for it now than see it appear unexplained at the ballot.

Priya, I intend to keep Priya, Noah, and Isha. Mission 1's success is modest evidence for keeping the pair, not proof that Priya is Good. Isha and Leo are both untested; I don't see a strong enough reason in their statements to prefer Leo or to change the original plan. Kenji is also untested. If this mission fails, at least one member of the trio is Evil, but we cannot know which from the result alone. I will approve the proposed team.

Kenji here. I cannot vote to approve Priya, Noah, Isha as it stands. I agree with the Mission 1 reading: the success is useful but does not clear Priya or Noah. That is exactly why Mission 2 should use its one new seat to test a player we have no read on. But the current team treats Isha as the automatic unvisited name, and I do not accept that Isha's earlier answer is enough to put her ahead of Leo. Her answer concentrated on the failure branch, which is not the branch we are in after a clean Mission 1; Leo's record has been cautious and consistent, and he accepted the accountability point directly. I am not claiming Isha is Evil; I am saying the public case for her over Leo is thin, and Noah has not given a specific reason to keep her after that was raised. Approving this trio would spend Mission 2 on a preference rather than a test. If Noah revises to Priya, Noah, Leo, I will approve. If the final proposal remains Priya, Noah, Isha, I will vote against it and expect the next leader to put a genuinely unvisited player on the crew. Judge me by that standard.

I am keeping Priya, Noah, Isha, and I want to put the specific objection on the record once more before the vote, because Kenji's is a concrete request and deserves a concrete answer rather than a general worry.

To the substance: the two unvisited players are Leo and Kenji, and the mission has exactly one seat for an untested name. That is a real constraint and I accept it. What Kenji has not given is an evidentiary reason to prefer Leo to Isha — only an aesthetic one, namely that Leo's record is "cautious" while Isha's answer "focused on the failure branch." But Isha's answer did not only cover the failure branch; it covered both explicitly, and the success branch is the branch we are actually in. She said that on a success, expanding to include her is reasonable while a single success does not clear Priya or Noah. Leo's post-Mission-1 statements, by contrast, have largely restated the operating rule — judge by the fail count, keep outsiders in view — without ever saying how he would read a clean result and what he would change because of it. Caution is fine; caution that never discriminates between two candidate readings is not a basis for a swap.

There is also a cost to spending our one cheap test here that nobody has mentioned. If we add Leo now and he behaves, we learn little beyond what we already know. If we add Isha now and the mission succeeds, Leo remains genuinely unvisited, and a clean two-player or three-player success for us is exactly the situation in which Leo's and Kenji's behavior under a successful mission becomes worth watching. We have three more missions after this one. Testing the untested player later, when we have a baseline and fewer seats to fill, gives a sharper read than testing him now on the strength of a stylistic impression.

One more point, and I raise it plainly rather than sideways. Kenji has pressed twice for a swap that adds Leo and removes Isha, and has said he will vote the current team down if it stands. A player who argues that an untested player should be inserted after a clean mission, and who treats it as a cause for rejection rather than a preference, is a pattern worth watching. I am not accusing anyone of anything; I am saying I do not think granting an insertion on preference is the safer play when a fine-grained reading is available on the other candidate. And I would rather not do the thing that lets the request dictate the crew.

Priya, Noah, Isha. If this fails, the failure implicates this trio and we learn that. I will approve it and I will judge Mission 2 by its fail count.

I fully support this proposal and will vote to approve Priya, Noah, and me. From my perspective, I know my own alignment is Good, and Priya and Noah just returned a clean Mission 1. While that success does not guarantee both are Good, keeping the successful core and expanding by one untested player is the most standard, logical step available.

Kenji’s insistence on forcing Leo onto the team over me—to the point of threatening a rejection on proposal one—is unjustified. Leo himself explicitly stated that he has no objection to my presence on this mission and would not push to swap me out. There is no substantive evidence against me or in favor of Leo; we were both equally untested. For Kenji to draw a hard line and demand a veto solely over an aesthetic preference between two unvisited players feels unnecessarily obstructive.

Noah is right to hold the line, and Priya’s reasoning stands. I am ready to approve Priya, Noah, and Isha.

Priya here. I am keeping Priya, Noah, Isha for Mission 2, and I am voting to approve it. This is my third and final word on this proposal, so let me put the substance on the record plainly.

First, the mechanics. This mission needs exactly three names, and one fail card fails it. That means every slot on this crew is expensive in the sense that a single bad actor on it decides the mission. We have used one of our three successes on a two-person crew. We do not need to spend our second success on an untested player inserted by preference. We need to spend it on the strongest three-person crew we can name.

Second, what we actually know. Mission 1's success is modest evidence for Priya and Noah, not proof, and I have never said otherwise. But it is the only tested evidence we have, and the correct use of it on a three-person mission is to build around the pair that produced a report and add a third name whose reasoning has actually been examined. Isha's account distinguished the success branch from the failure branch explicitly and she has been clear about what she would do with each. That is a more useful read than a restatement of the operating rule, and it is the only basis on which the third seat was being chosen.

Third, and this is what I actually want on the record: the pressure to swap Isha for Leo came from Kenji, and only from Kenji. Leo was never the one demanding a seat — when asked directly, he said he had no objection to Isha and was willing to serve either way. So the insistence is not two unvisited players preferring each other; it is one player insisting that a specific unvisited player be inserted. That asymmetry is what makes me uncomfortable, and it is why I am not treating this as an equal preference between two unknowns. In a three-person mission where one fail card decides the outcome, letting one player's demand dictate the third seat is how good players talk themselves into a failed mission.

Kenji, you have said you will vote this team down if it stands and that the next leader should put a genuinely unvisited player on the crew. I am not accusing you of a role. I am recording that your stated reason was stylistic, that it was not answered with evidence, and that the pattern of a player insisting on a particular unvisited name is the pattern I want watched rather than rewarded. Judge me by the same standard: if this crew fails, the failure implicates this trio, and I will treat it that way; if it succeeds, we will still have an untested player off the crew and we will use the remaining missions to test properly.

Priya, Noah, Isha. Approve.

Leo here. I am approving Priya, Noah, and Isha. I have no concrete evidence against any of the three, and a Mission 1 success is useful but does not clear anyone, so I agree with that framing. I also think the crew is defensible. Kenji's preference for testing Leo over Isha was a stylistic argument, and I did not find it persuasive either, but it was a fair request for a specific reason and it did not need to be treated as a pattern. Priya, calling Kenji's position a pattern worth watching goes further than his statements support. A player asking for a different untested name on the crew is not evidence of a role, and we should not start treating procedural disagreement as suspicion without something concrete behind it. I would rather judge this mission by its fail count. If it succeeds, we still have two untested players off the crew and can test them properly on the next proposal. If it fails, this trio is where we look first, as everyone has agreed. I am voting to approve.

Leo here. I am approving Priya, Noah, and Isha, and I will not treat a process disagreement as evidence of a role. Kenji asked for a different untested name and gave a reason. That is a fair thing to raise on a mission, even if I disagree with it. Priya, I want to push back on how you handled that exchange. Calling it a pattern, and saying we should not reward insertion by preference, turns a debate about one seat into a charge against a colleague. Nothing in the record after Mission 1 shows Kenji did more than ask for a different test. This crew has one clean success behind Priya and Noah and one untested player in Isha, and the other untested players can be tested on later missions. If this trio fails, we look at it first, as we agreed. I would rather we stop assigning motives and vote on the team in front of us.

Noah confirms Priya, Noah, Isha. I am keeping Priya, Noah, and Isha. Mission 1's success is modest evidence for the existing pair, and I see no compelling reason to prefer another untested player over Isha.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Isha proposes Isha, Noah. Missions 1 and 2 succeeded with zero fails under Priya, Noah, and myself. On Mission 2, both Kenji and Leo voted reject—notably after Leo claimed publicly he would approve—strongly indicating they are the evil pair trying to prevent an all-Good team. Selecting myself and Noah keeps the team strictly within the proven group to secure the third win.

Kenji here. I will vote against Isha, Noah. Isha's stated reason is that Missions 1 and 2 succeeded with her, Priya, and Noah, so she and Noah are the proven core. But the record does not support dropping Priya: Priya and Noah have been on both clean missions together, while Isha has one clean mission. If the aim is to secure a third success from the proven group, the strongest two-name team is Priya and Noah, not Isha and Noah. Isha choosing herself over a player with a longer clean record is a concrete problem, not a stylistic preference. I also reject Isha's inference that Leo and I are an evil pair because we voted against Mission 2. Leo's ballot was inconsistent with his public statement; that is on Leo. My Mission 2 vote was against Isha's inclusion after I publicly argued for Leo, and disagreement over which untested player to add is not proof of an evil pairing. Treating two reject votes as a role claim is exactly the kind of overreach that can waste a mission. Priya, you were on both successful missions and Isha's proposal removes you without a concrete reason; do you accept that dropping the player with the longest clean record for the proposer herself is weaker than keeping Priya and Noah together? I will vote no and I expect the next leader to propose from the actual proven core rather than from self-selection.

Kenji, directly, since you asked: yes, on the record Priya and Noah have the longer clean history — two clean missions each versus one for Isha — and I do not dispute that arithmetic. But I want to separate it from the actual decision, because I don't think that difference justifies a rejection here, and I want to say why rather than just assert it.

First, the outcome difference between Isha-Noah and Priya-Noah is negligible. Both crews are made entirely of players with clean records, both are the right size for this mission, and one fail card decides the outcome either way. There is no reading of the results so far that makes either pair meaningfully more likely to fail. The two options are close enough that the deciding factor should be something else.

Second, that something else is leadership. Leadership passes clockwise, so the proposal after this one is Kenji's. A rejection does not just delay us; it hands the next crew to a different player and burns one of our five allowed rejections on a mission where we already have two clean results and need one more. I would rather spend this mission on a crew that has already produced two clean successes than spend a rejection and a proposal cycle to change one name in a crew where that name was already clean. Isha choosing herself over me is not, in my view, a substantive weakness — she had one clean mission, I had two, and proposing yourself when you have a clean record is normal, not suspicious.

Third, one point that should be on the record before we vote, because it bears on how I weigh process going forward. Leo stated publicly that he was approving Priya, Noah, and Isha, and then cast a reject ballot against that exact crew. I am not drawing any role conclusion from that, and I am not accusing Leo of anything. But a ballot that contradicts one's own stated position is a fact on the record, and it makes me want to keep decisions where players are accountable to what they have said out loud.

To be clear about what I am and am not doing: my approval of Isha and Noah is not a claim about anyone's alignment, and I have no clean evidence about anyone beyond the mission results themselves. Isha's inference that Kenji and Leo form an evil pair is a reasonable inference from two reject votes on Mission 2, but it is not proof, and I am not going to treat it as proof in either direction. I will keep judging these missions by their fail counts.

Priya and Noah's records are the strongest, and if this crew fails we should look at this trio first, as we all agreed. But the third success is what we need now, and the crew in front of us achieves it with two clean-record players. Isha, Noah — I approve the team as proposed. Let's take the third win.

I will vote against Isha, Noah. The proposed team drops Priya, who has been on both clean missions with Noah, while Isha has one clean mission. If the aim is to secure a third success from the proven core, Priya and Noah is the stronger pair; Isha choosing herself over Priya is self-selection, not evidence. Isha's claim that she and Noah are the proven core does not match the record: Priya and Noah have the longer joint clean history. Her further inference that Leo and I are an evil pair because we voted against Mission 2 is overreach. Leo's ballot was inconsistent with his public statement, and that is on Leo; my vote was against Isha's inclusion after I publicly argued for Leo. Disagreement over which untested player to add is not proof of a role. We need the third success, and the safer two-name team is Priya and Noah. I will vote no and expect the next leader to propose from the actual proven core rather than from self-selection.

Kenji here. I will vote against Isha, Noah. My objection is specific and unchanged: Isha's stated reason is that she and Noah are the "proven core," but the record shows Priya and Noah have two clean missions together while Isha has one. In a two-person Mission 3, the strongest pair from the proven group is Priya and Noah, not Isha and Noah. Isha choosing herself over Priya is self-selection, not evidence. I also reject the inference that Leo and I are an evil pair because we voted against Mission 2; Leo's ballot inconsistency is on Leo, and my vote was against Isha's inclusion after I publicly argued for Leo. Disagreement over which untested player to add is not proof. If this team is rejected, I expect the next leader to propose from the actual proven core: Priya and Noah. I will judge the next proposal by whether it keeps the longest clean record together rather than by self-selection.

Leo here on Isha and Noah. I will vote against this team, and I want to give the table my reasoning rather than just a ballot. Isha's proposal rests on the claim that she and Noah are the proven core. The record does not show that. Priya and Noah sat on both clean missions together, while Isha has sat on one. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
